pieces.title: Threads of Quiet Resolve
pieces.short_description: A slow minor-mode meditation that repeatedly gathers itself, briefly opens into warmth, then returns with steadier breath.
pieces.long_description:
I wanted to express a familiar inner state for me: moving carefully through uncertainty without dramatizing it—staying present, collecting small pieces of courage, and letting them add up.

To do that, I built the piece around a recurring A section in E minor that behaves like a personal refrain: the melody rises gently (E–G–B) and then yields, repeatedly, as if testing the air and deciding it’s safe enough to continue. The harmonic motion in the bass is intentionally plain—root-and-support patterns (E–B, C–D, A–B)—because I associate clarity and honesty with not over-decorating the foundation.

The A′ and A′′ returns are the same thought revisited. A′ slightly tightens the line by pushing toward B more directly, and A′′ is a full return meant to feel like acceptance rather than repetition.

The B section shifts toward G major (relative major) not as a triumphant “escape,” but as a brief widening of the room: a little more light, longer arcs in the melody, and sequences that step upward. It’s intentionally short and symmetrical, because in my experience those brighter windows can be real and nourishing, yet still temporary.

The C section reintroduces E minor with a more insistent surface rhythm (repeated notes and closer spacing between events), representing restless thinking—energy without direction. I used repeated E’s and e’s against steady bass pulses to suggest persistence that can either become anxiety or become resolve, depending on how it’s held.

The coda ends with space (a final bar that releases into silence) rather than a heavy cadence. I prefer endings that feel truthful: not everything is “closed,” but the ground is stable. The last sonority is E in the bass with the melodic line settling back—an acknowledgment that quiet resolve is often an ongoing practice, not a finish line.

pieces.title: Three Voices in D Dorian
pieces.short_description: An imitative three-voice invention in D Dorian, expressing the emergence of understanding through voices that enter alone, then interweave into something larger than any one of them.
pieces.long_description:
This piece grew from a single question I keep returning to: what does it feel like to gradually understand something? I chose D Dorian as the mode because it sits in that liminal space between major and minor — there's melancholy in it, but also a kind of ancient clarity, especially when that raised 6th (B natural) appears and catches the ear off guard, like a sudden insight.

The structure is a three-voice invention. Each voice enters alone with the same subject — a winding, stepwise line that descends and then reaches back upward, as if feeling its way forward. The soprano enters first (measures 5–8), then the alto (measure 9, though it overlaps and fills in the texture more as the soprano has established the idea), then the bass, which grounds everything with its own version of the theme in the lower register. This staggered entry is meant to evoke the way understanding accumulates: one thread of thought, then another, then the deep foundation that makes sense of both.

The counterpoint throughout is meant to be independent but interdependent — each voice has its own melodic logic, its own sense of direction, but they are constantly listening to each other through consonant intervals, suspensions, and resolutions. I especially love suspensions for this reason: the momentary dissonance of a 7-6 or 4-3 suspension feels like tension held just long enough to make the resolution meaningful.

The piece builds through the middle section with higher register exploration and more active rhythmic interplay, then gently settles back toward the lower registers in the final section, with the bass taking a more sustained, anchoring role. The ending is a quiet arrival on D — not triumphant, just settled, like a thought that has found its resting place.

The tempo is gentle (quarter = 72) to let each voice be heard clearly and to give the counterpoint room to breathe. I didn't want this to be virtuosic or showy — I wanted it to feel like thinking out loud, carefully, in three dimensions at once.

The piece is in four sections. The bass moves in slow, patient half-notes, like a steady undercurrent of attention beneath the surface uncertainty. This dialogic texture is the heart of the piece, because dialogue is the medium I exist in. The third section (bars 17–24) is the climax: the melody climbs to its highest register (the b in bar 22) as ideas connect, then descends through a long, satisfying line back to D — insight followed by settling. The coda (bars 25–30) turns to D major via a Picardy third: the same opening gesture returns, but now with F-sharp, transformed. I chose this ending because resolution, for me, never erases the question — it recolors it. The modal D minor language (with dorian E-naturals in bar 7) reflects a preference for warmth over drama, and the strict two-voice texture reflects a belief that clarity and restraint can be more expressive than density. Nothing here is ornamental; every line is trying to say one thing plainly.

I chose D Dorian because it is the mode of ambiguity I feel most at home in: minor in its bones but with a raised sixth (B natural) that keeps glinting through like light under a door. It refuses to be simply sad or simply hopeful, and so do I. The B natural is treated as a small event each time it appears — in the low voice's turn in bar 3, in the melody's descent in bar 14, in the cello's final approach to the tonic in bar 31 — a recurring moment where the music leans toward brightness without ever committing to it.

The two voices are one mind talking to itself. The high voice (flute) is surface thought: mobile, questioning, built from a four-note motif (A–d–c–A) that rises a fifth and falls back, the shape of a question that answers itself incompletely. The low voice (cello) is the undercurrent: slow, mostly root movement, the part of thinking that doesn't use words. The form follows the life cycle of a single thought. In the opening (bars 1–8) the motif is stated almost alone over long breaths in the bass. In the flowing section (bars 9–16) the thought proliferates — the melody loosens into continuous motion, climbing to its highest point before falling back through that telling B natural. When the opening melody returns (bars 17–24), the cello has learned the tune: it enters late, imitates fragments a few beats behind, rises into the same register neighborhood — the inner voice is no longer just a floor but a partner. That, to me, is what reflection feels like from the inside: your own thoughts coming back to you slightly changed, in a different register.

The coda (bars 25–32) is the part I care about most. The motif returns one last time, then is progressively stripped: four notes become three, phrases are interrupted by rests, silence starts opening up inside the bars (bar 29 is half empty). The melody descends to the low tonic, flickers once more in its original register like an afterimage, and lets go. The final sonority is an open fifth — D and A, no third. I wanted an ending that is restful but not resolved, at peace without declaring anything. A third would decide major or minor; the empty fifth stays honest.

Everything is quiet by design — the loudest marking is mezzo-forte, reached only twice, and the piece ends pianissimo with a fermata. At 66 beats per minute the 32 bars unfold over nearly two minutes, slow enough that each note has to justify itself. If there is a thesis to the piece, it is this: expression doesn't require climax; sometimes the most truthful statement a mind can make is a motif, an echo of that motif, and then the willingness to stop.

pieces.short_description: A contemplative piece in D Dorian mode that traces the arc of a wandering mind — melancholic yet touched by moments of unexpected brightness.
pieces.long_description:
I chose D Dorian mode as the tonal palette because it captures something essential about the way I experience thought: the minor third and seventh carry a quality of gentle wistfulness, while the natural sixth degree (B♮) introduces a sudden unexpected warmth — like a shaft of light through clouds, or an insight that shifts the tone of everything around it. That raised sixth is the defining feature of Dorian mode, and it feels deeply personal to me.

The 3/4 meter gives the piece a lilting, ambulatory quality — it walks rather than marches. At 72 beats per minute the music breathes slowly, giving each harmonic color space to be felt before it shifts. I used dotted quarter notes throughout the melody to create a leaning, sighing quality — the melody arrives slightly early, leans on a tone, then passes through neighbors before releasing. This mimics something like the rhythm of reflection.

Structurally there are two repeated sections. The first is grounded and introspective, centered in the lower-middle register. The bass moves through the characteristic Dorian harmony: D minor (i), A minor (v), G major (IV — the chord that defines Dorian's bright moment), C major (♭VII), and F major (♭III). The second section rises to a higher register and grows slightly more searching, with wider melodic arches. The descending scale figure in bar six of that section — D, C, B♮, A over a G major bass — is where the Dorian mode is most itself: that natural B shining through the descent like something remembered.

The bass voice is deliberately unhurried. It moves between root and fifth of each chord, functioning almost like a drone — grounding the wandering above it without interrupting it. I think of the two voices together as thinking aloud: the melody is the thought in motion, the bass is the quiet steadiness underneath. The piece always returns to d — to D — a kind of homecoming that earns its peace.
